records.title: 5G Network Management for Lunar and Deep Space Communications
records.summary: To identify the essential network management functions for a successful lunar communication architecture by simulating how data traffic is automatically managed and protected over unreliable space connections leveraging terrestrial wireless technologies. Benefits: State of the art tools include modeling of lunar surface propagation, line of sight between assets, network traffic loading, and user data protocol simulation. They lack network performance monitoring and control functions. This project will assess network management protocol standards and extend the simulation framework to evaluate how they can be implemented in the end-to-end lunar network. Results will develop understanding of current 3GPP network management standards, enhance simulation tools for lunar scenarios and improve simulation fidelity of Moon Base end-to-end data flows.
keywords: Communications, Navigation, and Orbital Debris Tracking and Characterization Systems

records.title: A Catalog of Dispersive Ionospheric and Plasmaspheric Arcs from Cislunar and Lunar-surface GNSS Radio Occultations
records.summary: This dataset is a catalog of 263 dispersive arcs induced by ionospheric and plasmaspheric occultation observed in GNSS signals recorded by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE) payload during Blue Ghost Mission 1 (BGM1), in cislunar space and on the lunar surface. Occultation arcs are identified and classified as ingress, egress or tangent by combining independently GPS and Galileo dual-frequency observables and computing the rate of the total electron content (ROT) and ROT index (ROTI), and are validated through a geometric criterion based on the grazing altitude of the tangent point. No distinction is made between the ionospheric and plasmaspheric contributions to each arc, which is treated as a single dispersive signature. For each arc, the catalog provides timing, grazing altitude, summary ROT/ROTI/$Δ$STEC attributes, the geomagnetic activity level, and time series of leveled slant total electron content (STEC), not corrected for instrumental biases, ROT, ROTI, tangent-point position and local time. The HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format version 5) file contains a header with dataset-wide metadata and per-class statistics, and one entry per arc. It enables rapid selection of occultation arcs for statistical studies and targeted analyses, and complements ground-based and low Earth orbit radio-occultation data during the declining phase of solar cycle 25.

records.title: A Differential Geometric Approach to Autonomous Navigation
records.summary: Precision landing technology is vital to the future of space exploration, especially for the Artemis program's goal of a sustained lunar presence. Regular robotic landings will require significant advances in the reliability, precision, and efficiency of the navigation algorithms used in this phase of flight. Three problems are especially pressing -- quantifying system nonlinearity, characterizing the convergence regions of initial orbit determination methods, and representing non-Gaussian uncertainties. Differential geometry is a branch mathematics that develops the tools to do calculus on curved surfaces. Many current navigation algorithms use Euclidean (flat) geometry to describe dynamical and measurement models that are inherently non-Euclidean. Differential geometry is uniquely suited to address these three research gaps because it can better analyze the underlying geometry of these models. This greater insight should result in improvements in the efficiency, robustness, and/or precision of the navigation algorithms used in autonomous landings.

records.title: A Knowledge-Centric Communication For Autonomous Cislunar Networks
records.summary: Future lunar infrastructure requires communication as a persistent service rather than a mission specific capability. Communication, digital twin, and artificial intelligence (AI) research have advanced autonomy independently while largely assuming that system state can eventually be reconciled with ground truth. Cislunar communication violates this assumption because propagation delay is fundamentally limited by the speed of light, visibility is governed by orbital geometry, and autonomous decisions often precede confirming observations. Here we introduce a knowledge-centric communication framework in which a digital twin continuously integrates delayed observations, communication physics, learned models, uncertainty quantification, and mission objectives into an evolving Operational Knowledge State. To quantify what is known, how uncertain it remains, and how current it is, we define two quantities over the fused Bayesian belief maintained for each communication link: \emph{Knowledge Entropy}, the differential entropy of the posterior belief, and \emph{Knowledge Freshness}, which generalizes Age of Information (AoI) from a single information stream to the temporal validity of the fused Operational Knowledge State. We prove that distributed knowledge fusion systematically improves operational knowledge by reducing uncertainty and demonstrate its importance for mission success through simulations and comparisons with flight data from the Longjiang-2 lunar micro-satellite.

records.title: A low-SWaP timing system for distributed in-orbit and planetary surface platforms
records.summary: Low-cost missions in cislunar space demand positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) and communications capabilities that are not achieved with current onboard timing systems. No space-rated atomic standard fits the size, power, and stability requirements for these applications. Accordingly, this work addresses the technology gap in precise timing systems for small spacecraft operating in the cislunar domain. This work proposes the investigation of an ensemble of compact atomic clocks onboard and distributed across in-orbit and planetary surface platforms. Such an ensemble would realize the timing stability of the best clock across the linked platforms at medium-term to long-term averaging intervals. Furthermore, the overall reliability of the timing signal will increase, reducing its sensitivity to environmental perturbations seen by the individual clocks. Particularly, the impact of the ensemble in a lunar PNT satellite system will inform the performance of the navigation system. The ability to steer a local reference oscillator on the platforms directly to this ensemble time will alleviate the burden of ground monitoring and broadcast correction updates traditionally utilized in Global Navigation Satellite Systems. Therefore, this work will have critical impacts to the size, weight, power, cost, and precision of lunar PNT systems. The key contributions of this investigation will be (1) a computer-based model equipped with optimal ensemble algorithms and informed with data gathered through lunar mission datasets and hardware testing, and (2) a preliminary testbed to evaluate ensemble behavior emulating dynamical and environmental impacts. Methods proposed in this work involve periodic corrections from weak GNSS signals, clock comparison via pulsed optical and RF intersatellite links (ISLs), and corrections for special and general relativistic effects. Algorithm development, simulation analyses, and hardware testing will be conducted. The plethora of datasets now available from lunar missions, such as LuGRE, will inform realistic error models for this work.

records.title: A study on the contribution of the interplanetary medium in radio occultation experiments
records.summary: Irregularities in electron density within the interplanetary medium (IPM) can cause fluctuations in the Doppler frequency of spacecraft radio signals. The amplitude of these fluctuations depends on factors such as the carrier frequency, propagation geometry, and link configuration. However, quantitative characterization of these effects across different frequencies in various occultation experiments is currently limited. We analyze five complementary datasets: two-way S-band observations from Chandrayaan-3 outside the lunar ionosphere, two-way S-band data from Chandrayaan-2 during lunar occultation, one-way S/X band measurements from the Venus Express Radio Science (VeRa)/Akatsuki Radio Science (Akatsuki) under IPM-only conditions, and one-way X-band Akatsuki data during solar occultation. The Chandrayaan-3 and Akatsuki IPM observations isolate IPM effects by excluding contributions from planetary atmospheres, the lunar ionosphere, and, except during solar occultation, the solar corona. Chandrayaan-3 data sample dynamically evolving Earth-Moon geometries and exhibit weak, mHz-level Doppler fluctuations, while Chandrayaan-2 observations provide near-lunar plasma benchmarks with higher amplitudes, during quiet time solar and geomagnetic conditions. Akatsuki and VeRa's IPM-only measurements capture long-path interplanetary effects, whereas Akatsuki solar occultation data reveal strong coronal signatures. Power spectral density analysis indicates Kolmogorov-like turbulence for lunar occultation and solar occultation cases, while IPM-only spectra show low-amplitude fluctuations. These results quantify the IPM contribution to Doppler noise, demonstrate the enhanced plasma sensitivity of two-way coherent links, and provide constraints relevant to turbulence modelling, precision spacecraft tracking, and the interpretation of radio occultation experiments.

records.title: Antenna Metrology at the NASA Glenn Research Center: Advancements in Antenna Characterization and Communications Systems Testing
records.summary: Antenna metrology has been and continues to be a key aspect in the process of antenna design, simulation, fabrication, and characterization. Current work at the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) in support of space and aeronautics projects requires the thorough verification of antenna performance via experimental metrology of antennas being developed for lunar communications under the Artemis and Moon-to-Mars program, for aeronautics applications such as the emerging Advanced Air Mobility (AAM)/Urban Air Mobility (UAM) ecosystem, and for other related applications. This paper discusses the antenna metrology capabilities at GRC including the new Horizontal Planar Near Field Range (HPNF), and the new Compact Antenna Test Range (CATR), and the Portable Laser Guided Robotic Metrology (PLGRM) capability, together with a brief discussion of the preliminary results of the first antennas tested in the ranges.

records.title: Asteroids Impacting the Solar System Planets and the Moon. III. Real Impacts from Known Objects and LSST Discovery Predictions
records.summary: Impact rates predicted using pre-impact source-population models and those inferred from observations disagree by a factor of a few to $\sim200$ across the Solar System planets and the Moon. An exciting opportunity for an additional observational constraint is the discovery of asteroids before impact and their tracking until impact. We evaluate this prospect based on both known objects and forecasts of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). First, we identify impacts from known objects, confirming multiple past cases and predicting two coming impacts: 2015 FK488, a $\sim1.8$ km Centaur whose nominal orbit predicts an impact with Jupiter in $\sim200$ yr, and 2022 KG1, a $ 10$ m) and $\sim300$ future Jupiter impactors ($>10$ m), with a wider range on both ends for discovery-to-collision lead times. These results demonstrate that LSST can identify a subset of planetary impactors years to centuries before collision, providing a new observational pathway for testing source-population models and the impact-rate mismatch.

records.title: BEVIO: Efficient Bird's-Eye-View based Sparse-Update Visual-Inertial Odometry for Lunar Day-Night Navigation
records.summary: Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) provides smooth, high-rate state estimates and has been widely used for robotic navigation in both terrestrial and planetary applications. However, its performance is typically dependent on the frequency of visual updates, which is a challenge for planetary rovers operating under extreme resource constraints and low frame rates. This work investigates enabling reliable VIO with very sparse visual updates for lunar rover applications, addressing both day and night-time operations where feature associations become especially difficult under self-illumination conditions. We propose a Bird's Eye View (BEV)-based image matching scheme that remains robust to larger inter-frame motions and more reliable feature matching despite significant visual appearance changes. We extensively evaluate our proposed approach, BEVIO, through high-fidelity photorealistic lunar and real-time robotic experiments conducted using a half-scale lunar rover, in a long-term day-night deployment at Plaster City, CA, USA. The results demonstrate that our method enables reliable day and nighttime self-illuminated traverses at visual update rates as low as 0.25 Hz, underscoring its suitability for navigation on power- and compute-limited lunar rovers.

records.title: Beyond Sgr A* and M87*: Sub-Microarcsecond Black Hole Shadow Detection via Lunar-based Extremely Long Baseline Interferometry
records.summary: The 1.3 mm ground-based very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) array Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), is limited by Earth's diameter, restricting horizon-scale imaging to only M87* and Sgr A*. Extending baselines to the Moon would achieve ~0.7 microarcsecond angular resolution at 230 GHz, enabling shadow detection for many more supermassive black holes (SMBHs). The concept is motivated by space VLBI missions and lunar exploration, including the ongoing Lunar Orbit VLBI EXperiment (LOVEX) aboard QueQiao-2 (Chang'E-7) and the planned International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). We assess shadow detectability for 31 SMBHs with predicted large angular sizes, assuming optically thin emission at 230 GHz, exploring different telescope locations and antenna sizes. Assuming a telescope at the lunar antipode, we simulate the Moon-Earth (u,v) coverage and show that sources near the Moon's orbital plane yield projected baselines spanning a wide range, enabling sampling of the first visibility null - a key shadow signature. Using a geometric ring model, we identify six shadow-detectable candidates: M104, NGC 5077, and NGC 1052 are detectable with a 5 m lunar-based telescope; PGC 049940 with 10 m; NGC 524 with 20 m; and NGC 5252 with 40 m. If additional space telescopes fill the baseline coverage gaps between Moon and Earth, 14 candidates are detectable for the n=1 photon-ring region with a lunar-based telescope up to 40 m. These results provide a clear scientific and technical motivation for lunar-based telescopes in future black hole shadow studies.

records.title: Black Hole Binary Detection Landscape for the Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna (LILA): Signal-to-Noise Calculations & Science Cases
records.summary: The Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna (LILA) is a proposed gravitational-wave project aiming to take full advantage of the Moon's environment to access the deci-Hz band and detect intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) binaries of mass $\sim 10^2-10^6 \, M_{\odot}$ (arXiv:2508.11631). With an observational period of 4 years, LILA can extend its IMBH detection horizon to the very early Universe, directly probing the first population of massive black holes ($z \sim 20-30$). LILA could also detect intermediate-mass-ratio inspiral systems with a total mass of $\sim 10^4 - 10^6 \, M_{\odot}$ and a mass ratio of $\sim 10^{-4} - 10^{-2}$. LILA can discover IMBH binaries months to years before merger with measurable eccentricity residuals retained from their formation, providing crucial early warning for multi-messenger and multi-band follow-up. The high SNR ($\gtrsim 100$) events detectable with LILA would enable strong-field tests of gravity. With these capabilities, LILA will provide important insights into the formation and evolution of massive black holes, as well as the astrophysical environments and evolutionary pathways of black hole binaries. LILA will also complement current LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA detections of pair-instability mass gap events, hierarchical merger candidates, and light IMBH mergers, while expanding the upper envelope of discovered black holes with stellar origin to masses of $\gtrsim 250 \, M_{\odot}$.

records.title: CAPSTONE Demonstration of Real-Time Autonomous Navigation Using One-Way Radiometric Measurements
records.summary: Real-time onboard navigation using one-way radiometric measurements in a Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO) about the Moon is demonstrated onboard the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment (CAPSTONE) mission. One-way forward pseudorange and integrated Doppler measurements are derived from CAPSTONE’s Iris transponder, which has been paired with a chip-scale atomic clock (CSAC) to provide a stable timing reference for navigation. Previous works by Todd Ely formulate and demonstrate one-way navigation with this configuration using CAPSTONE flight telemetry and tracking data to form a ground-based solution. This paper describes the first time it has been demonstrated onboard in real-time. Forward signals originate from NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN) and do not include Earth transmit time, ground station ID, or true transmit frequency, which are necessary to process one-way forward measurements. In lieu of this, two-way DSN-based radiometric measurements are uplinked to CAPSTONE to estimate a truth solution in near-real-time and provide the missing information for one-way measurement processing. Both the one-way and two-way solution states and measurement biases are estimated in a single filter powered by the Goddard Enhanced Onboard Navigation System (GEONS), embedded in the autonomous Navigation, Guidance, and Control (autoNGC) flight software. GEONS uses an upper-diagonal (UD) factorized extended Kalman filter (EKF) to process measurements and estimate states and measurement biases. Despite 20+ years of flight heritage in processing GPS, pulsar X-ray, and optical measurements for Earth-orbiting missions, this is the first time GEONS has been used to process one-way radiometric measurements in a lunar NRHO in flight. The GEONS Ground MATLAB Simulation (GGMS) tool suite was used to prototype flight telemetry processing and measurement formation algorithms, simulate filter performance using real flight data, and tune the filter for the flight demonstration. The flight configuration was simulated using the autoNGC software-in-the-loop (SIL) and processor-in-the-loop (PIL) test configurations. This paper documents the formulation of measurement formation algorithms, pre-flight analysis using flight data, autoNGC SIL/PIL testing results, flight results, and post-flight analysis.

records.title: Cislunar Orbit Determination via Intercepted Communication Signals
records.summary: Abstract This study shows the feasibility of positioning one or more satellites in orbit around the Earth-Moon Lagrange Point One (L1) to intercept radio frequency (RF) signals and determine the position and velocity of spacecraft near the lunar surface, such as lunar orbiters or surface vehicles. It is assumed that the tracked vehicle will occasionally communicate directly with Earth using standard RF bands. While system performance at L1 depends on the architecture, including hardware and the number of satellites, initial results indicate that three optimized satellites can achieve position and velocity errors of about 1100 meters and 0.1 meters per second, respectively. With two satellites, errors are around 1500 meters and 0.14 meters per second. For a single satellite optimized for maximum convergence, the system can complete orbitdetermination with an 87% success rate, and errors are approximately 2500 meters and 0.29 meters persecond. When considering lunar surface targets, the position estimates improve toaround 300 meters due to the target’s constant inertial velocity. The study suggests that a small number of passive observers at the Earth-Moon "communications gate" can provide valuable Cislunar Space Domain Awareness with minimal infrastructure.

records.title: CisLunarSense: Opportunistic ISAC for Debris Detection at the Lunar Gateway
records.summary: We propose CisLunarSense, an opportunistic integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) framework that exploits the Lunar Gateway's Ka-band relay for monostatic debris detection, addressing the absence of cislunar space situational awareness infrastructure beyond the reach of ground-based radars. Using NASA/ESA-documented system parameters with author-selected sensing settings and a CR3BP-based 9:2 near-rectilinear halo orbit model, we derive the orbit-phase-dependent Cramér--Rao bound under OFDM inter-carrier interference, quantify a 36~dB cislunar sensing advantage over a ground-based Ka-band reference, and design a velocity-adaptive processor with mode switching at 337~m/s. Gateway operational debris ($v_\mathrm{rel} < 50$~m/s) is detectable within 700~km with over 30~minutes of warning; external threats ($v_\mathrm{rel}$ up to 500~m/s) remain detectable within 400--630~km. An orbit-phase-adaptive allocation reduces the sensing duty cycle from 60\% to 19\%, increasing relay throughput from 44 to 90~Mbps. A closed-form sensing outage probability for $K$-CPI non-coherent integration under Swerling~I fluctuation shows that the 10\%-outage detection range reaches 91\% of the deterministic maximum at the nominal operating point $K = 16$.

records.title: Communication Delays in Cislunar Space: Aims and Methods of a Laboratory Study Examining EIHSO and Team Risks
records.summary: The aim of the study is to investigate the effects of different time delays in the range of 0-12 second one-way communication. The EIHSO risk team focused on the implementation of a communication delay technology infrastructure, development of nominal and off-nominal spaceflight-relevant experimental tasks and prototypes, and identification of EIHSO-related performance measures and outcomes. The TEAM risk team focused on identification and recruiting of appropriate crew-like subjects, development of Qualtrics surveys for data collection, and identification of Team-related functioning and performance measures and outcomes.

records.title: Compact Optical Method for Long-range, Inexpensive Network Communication
records.summary: COMLINC uses customized optics and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) to provide a dramatically lower SWaP-C system than the optical communications State of the Art. The first two years produced a low-cost optical ground station that can track a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite and multiple prototype LED transmitters. One of the transmitters was launched into LEO during year 2 and will attempt to demonstrate a LEO downlink (increasing technology to TRL 6). During year 3, this project will further develop COMLINC technology by 1) developing uplink capability for COMLINC and 2) performing a trade study on potential applications of COMLINC with associated unit testing focusing on lunar surface conditions (e.g., dust, range, lighting, technology alternatives, etc.) Benefits: By adding uplink capability, COMLINC enables true bi‑directional optical communication at dramatically lower SWAP‑C than current state‑of‑the‑art optical systems. This approach can deliver data rates comparable to, or exceeding, traditional RF communications while avoiding RF‑spectrum regulatory constraints that significantly slow mission readiness timelines. Through targeted trade studies and unit testing under lunar‑relevant conditions, COMLINC can better define its operational envelope and mature into a low‑SWAP‑C architecture suitable for diverse lunar applications. Potential uses include ...

records.title: Cross Layer Spectrum Aware Cognitive Control Plane and Intelligent Routing Engine
records.summary: AiRANACULUS and partners proposes an innovative Cross Layer Spectrum Aware Cognitive Control Plane and Intelligent Routing Engine (CLAIRE) solution to increase mission science data return, improve resource efficiencies for NASA missions and communication networks and ensure resilience in the unpredictable space environment. An Autonomous Intelligent Reconfiguration system is envisioned to sense, detect, adapt, and learn from its experiences and environment to optimize the communications capabilities for the lunar surface, lunar proximity and cislunar network infrastructure. The NASA CLAIRE CCRPP project will enhance the TRL (5 to 7) and MRL (4 to 6) of the technologies developed through NASA CLAIRE project (Contract #80NSSC21C0510 same name adopted) which completed Phase II and Phase II-E. The CCRPP will also leverage the work been carried out on NASA INSPiRE Project (Contract # 80NSSC22CA141) where Phase II has been completed and Phase II-E is on-going. CLAIRE provides wide-band Radio Frequency (RF) sensing, cognitive control plane as an APP, interference mitigation techniques, autonomous channel assignments and congestion aware packet forwarding. INSPiRE builds on CLAIRE and provides spectrum and interference aware routing, network slicing over heterogeneous multivendor network to maintain Quality of Service (QoS), policy-based prioritization and INSPiRE enhanced HDTN Contact Graph Routing (CGR). CLAIRE engages in local link level optimization, INSPiRE engages in global optimization of the network for a wide variety of users. In this project, CLAIRE and INSPiRE will interface with the Glenn Research Center (GRC) Cognitive Engine (CE). CLAIRE and INSPiRE functionality will be integrated into TES CubeSat, and flight tested. CLAIRE and INSPiRE will be integrated into Nokia Banshee Mobile Radio (BMR) and 5G O-RAN platform provided by Nvidia / Radisys / Juniper. Together, this will demonstrate resilient wireless operation on lunar surface and lunar proximity networks. Benefits: CLAIRE and INSPiRE provide following Capabilities and Applications: • CLAIRE APP enabled Cognitive Control Plane provides spectrum and network situational awareness. Application Layer Heartbeat (HTBT) messages may be sent over any IP-enabled network. This enables Link Optimization using Dynamic Spectrum Access / Dynamic Channel Assignment and Dynamic Bandwidth Adaptation. • Wide-Band RF Sensing with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning enables detection and characterization of interference with >90% Probability of Correct Classification of Interference with 90% throughput improvement ...

records.title: Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking in Cislunar Space
records.summary: DTN (Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking) is the foundation of NASA's LunaNet architecture, which will enable the robust communications, navigation, and networking capabilities needed to establish a long-term presence on the moon. DTN is a network architecture composed of several different protocols that are designed to provide internetworking functionality and standardized multi-hop, end-to-end data delivery in highly stressed environments that are not optimal for traditional Internet Protocols. Bundle Protocol (BP) version 7, a store-and-forward protocol intended to run at the application layer on top of convergence layer protocols, provides the key delay tolerance functionality of DTN and is designed to handle intermittent connectivity, long delays, bit errors, and other common issues in a space-based network. The CCSDS (Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems) Custody Transfer specification provides the disruption tolerance by guaranteeing reliable delivery through bundle acknowledgements. NASA Goddard’s implementation of BP version 7 and the related specifications is provided by a generic C-language library (BPLib) that can be integrated within the standard core Flight System (cFS) architecture with a cFS application (BPNode), both of which are open source. Its design emphasizes customization at the build level, in-flight configurability through commands and tables, multi-threading, resource limitations, performance optimization, and various other considerations key to flight software. It leverages the open-source libraries QCBOR, to encode and decode bundles, and SQLite, to provide a storage database for bundles that cannot be immediately forwarded or delivered. Future work on Goddard’s BPNode includes support for additional convergence layer protocols, integration with the Bundle Protocol Security library to provide end-to-end data protection, and more. BPNode has been deployed on the CAPSTONE CubeSat (Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment) currently in orbit around the moon, and experimentation onboard the spacecraft has demonstrated the ability to scale BPNode down to link rates as low as 2 Kbps, while lab experimentation on more powerful machines has demonstrated its ability to scale up to data rates of almost 900 Mbps with large bundles. This presentation will discuss the results of on-orbit DTN experimentation including uplink and downlink bundle flows, bundle transfers using the CCSDS Custody Transfer standard, and lessons learned from the cislunar experimentation in this challenging environment. As infrastructure in cislunar space continues to be built up in support of the ongoing Artemis missions, a cFS solution for DTN will allow for the deployment of increasingly complex networking architectures on flight software in and around the moon.
keywords: Space Communications, Spacecraft Communications, Command and Tracking

records.title: Determination of the longitude difference between Baghdad and Khwarezm using a lunar eclipse (the method of Abu Rayhan al-Biruni and Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani)
records.summary: This paper examines how, in the tenth century, medieval Iranian scholars Abu Rayhan al-Biruni and Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani determined the difference in geographical longitude between the cities of Baghdad and Khwarezm through simultaneous observation of a lunar eclipse. Brief academic biographies of these scholars are presented, with emphasis on their contributions to mathematics and astronomy. The study discusses the importance of determining geographical coordinates - especially longitude - in the science of the 10th-11th centuries, provides an overview of the methods of coordinate determination available at the time, and highlights the problem of synchronizing remote observations prior to the advent of electronic communication. Particular attention is devoted to a detailed analysis of the method based on observing a lunar eclipse to simultaneously measure longitude differences: the necessary conditions and organization of the experiment, the instruments employed, the mathematical calculations, and error estimates are described. The longitude difference obtained by al-Biruni and al-Buzjani is compared with modern values. The conclusion discusses the scientific significance of this method for the history of science and astronomy.

records.title: Development of a Compact, Wide-Field X-ray Navigation Sensor for Simultaneous Multi-Pulsar Tracking
records.summary: Deep space exploration is currently constrained by a heavy reliance on the Deep Space Network (DSN) for navigation and timing services. As the volume of lunar and planetary missions increases, the DSN bandwidth is approaching saturation, creating a critical bottleneck for future exploration. The central objective of this research is to alleviate this dependency by developing an autonomous X-ray navigation (XNAV) system specifically designed for the resource-constrained platforms of Small Satellites. While XNAV technology (using the consistent pulses of neutron stars as a galactic GPS) has been proven on large missions such as SEXTANT, current architectures use bulky focusing optics that are too heavy and power-hungry for small spacecraft. This proposal aims to overcome these barriers by validating a compact, wide-field instrument capable of determining spacecraft Position, Velocity, and Time (PVT) without the need for heavy telescopes or active cooling. The proposed method utilizes an architecture that replaces traditional grazing-incidence mirrors with a Coded Aperture Mask (CAM). This "lens-less" imaging technique operates on the principle of shadow-casting, allowing for a lightweight, flat profile that offers a wide Field-of-View. Behind the mask, the instrument utilizes Timepix3 hybrid pixel detectors coupled with Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) sensors. This specific detector technology allows for single-photon counting with high timing precision at room temperature, enabling the detection of the soft X-ray flux of Millisecond Pulsars down to 5 keV without complex cooling systems. To process the data, the research will develop a "Spatial-Temporal Folding" algorithm. This custom processing pipeline will simultaneously track multiple pulsars within the wide field-of-view, using Maximum-Likelihood Expectation-Maximization (MLEM) decoding to disentangle their signals from the cosmic X-ray background. The research plan progresses from high-fidelity GEANT4 simulations to hardware procurement, followed by rigorous laboratory characterization and thermal vacuum testing to quantify the navigation error budget. The significance of this proposed work lies in its potential to democratize deep space autonomy. This project directly addresses the NASA Civil Space Shortfalls regarding Deep Space Autonomous Navigation and Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) for Small ...

records.title: Earth-baseline VLBI restores the observability of a lunar surface station in joint orbit-and-clock determination
records.summary: Lunar positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) is moving from concept to hardware, ESA's Moonlight/LCNS, NovaMoon reference stations, LunaNet, and Coordinated Lunar Time, all reducing to one estimation core: fix the orbits and clocks of the lunar infrastructure and tie them to an Earth/inertial frame. We ask which measurements make a surface station's absolute position observable, and prove the answer. In a snapshot batch fit, the internal observables (station-to-satellite and inter-satellite ranging plus clock-sync) constrain only relative geometry and leave a six-dimensional rigid-body datum defect: three translations and three rotations of the cluster. The clocks are fully observable, so the defect is purely positional, and closing it needs a tie to the Earth frame. Two such ties exist and are not interchangeable. An indirect tie (Earth-to-satellite ranging through the constellation) reaches the station only when the satellite geometry is rich; a direct tie (an Earth-baseline VLBI delay to the station beacon) fixes it regardless. This gives a conditional design law, not a single number: VLBI restores absolute observability when the constellation cannot supply it, and merely sharpens the bound when it can. For a sparse three-satellite constellation the station lies in the null space of the Fisher information until VLBI is added, reaching a Cramer-Rao bound of 20.1 m; for a rich six-satellite constellation VLBI tightens the bound from 23.2 m to 9.7 m. A single-epoch baseline informs at most two of three axes, so the datum closes at three non-collinear Earth stations. The Gauss-Newton estimator attains the bound (efficiency 1.02), with a 91x median station-error improvement in the sparse regime. The FIM/CRLB engine is validated against NumPy and published closed forms; the lunar application stays modelled, every figure deterministic and reproducible.

records.title: Eclipse Observables for Navigation in Cislunar Space
records.summary: Autonomous navigation independent of Earth-based tracking remains a challenge for spacecraft operating in cislunar space. This paper proposes onboard eclipse detection as an opportunistic measurement set to supplement the state estimation of cislunar trajectories. Penumbral and umbral entry and exit times detected from standard power telemetry are formulated as implicit zero-measurements on the boundaries of second-order shadow cones computed from planetary ephemerides. These observables are processed in an unscented Kalman filter. The event-time uncertainty that weights each measurement is derived from physical sources excluded in the spherical body model, including telemetry sampling, Earth's atmosphere, and topography/oblateness of the occulting body. The approach is demonstrated both in simulation for an $L_1$ halo orbit and with flight telemetry and orbit determination products from the CAPSTONE spacecraft during the January 2026 lunar eclipse, where umbral contacts timed directly from the power telemetry agree with the geometric contacts to within one sample interval. In both cases, hardware-free eclipse event timing shows utility in uncertainty reduction, especially as the initial solution quality is degraded.

records.title: Electrical coupling of a horizontal dipole antenna to a dielectric half-space: applications to radio astronomy from the lunar surface
records.summary: The far side of the Moon, shielded from terrestrial radio frequency interference and beyond the influence of Earth's ionosphere, should offer a uniquely quiet environment for radio astronomy and cosmological experiments. The radio sky below 30 MHz is largely unexplored and is thought to contain spectral signatures of new physics in the early, high-redshift Universe. Achieving precision measurements in this band requires accurate understanding of antenna performance and systematics. For upcoming lunar surface radio astronomy missions, this modeling will be challenging because antennas will deploy at heights that are only a small fraction of a wavelength above the lunar regolith, where strong coupling between the antenna and the surface can significantly alter impedance, radiation patterns, and efficiency. The challenge is compounded by the layered dielectric structure of the regolith and the tendency for permittivity to increase with depth, both of which are difficult to represent faithfully in numerical simulations. In this work, we review theoretical predictions for the behavior of a simple horizontal dipole above a dielectric half-space, representing the lunar regolith, and compare them with simulation results obtained using the Ansys HFSS integral equation solver. We quantify how the antenna impedance and beam pattern couple to the sky for a representative lunar surface radio astronomy experiment. The results show that surface induced effects decrease rapidly, even for modest increases in antenna height above the regolith. Conversely, a dipole antenna placed on or very near the lunar surface will exhibit complex spectral response that renders systematics control very difficult without detailed information on regolith properties.

records.title: Enhancing Performance and Communication for Distributed Teams During Lunar Spacewalks
records.summary: Research focuses on studying distributed multiteam performance of surface Extravehicular Activity (EVA) in a simulate, analog environment, operating under communication latencies and bandwidth limitations. Outcomes center on developing countermeasures that enable effective communication, facilitate EVA resource management, and enhance overall team performance in Moon-to-Mars EVA scenarios.

records.title: Evaluation of passive radio sounding of icy moons based on a radar equation
records.summary: Abstract Passive radar sounding is one of the ways to observe surfaces and subsurfaces of planetary objects through reflection of natural radio emissions. Using observations of Radio and Plasma Investigations (RPWI) aboard Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE), we have a plan to apply this technique to observe Jovian auroral radiation reflected on icy moons. For feasibility studies, we derived an expanded radar equation for planetary radio waves reflected on the moon’s surface, including the loss due to the moon’s spherical shape and scattering by surface roughness. Using this equation, we estimated the power and polarization characteristics of reflected radio emissions in two cases; terrestrial auroral kilometric radiation (AKR) reflected on the lunar surface and Jovian Hectometric radiation (HOM) reflected on the Ganymede surface. We showed the quantitative feasibility of the observation capability and potential of polarization measurements for detecting the permittivity of a surface. Additionally, we compared the estimation of the lunar case with a real case of AKR reflection observed using Lunar Radar Sounder (LRS) aboard Kaguya. The observed power ratio of reflected AKR to incident one was 2–5%, estimated from the interference fringe in the observed frequency-time diagram. This observed value agreed with the estimation from our radar equation.

records.title: Examination of the Joint Augmented Reality (AR) Navigation System for Lunar Surface Operations
records.summary: Delays in communication between ground support in Mission Control and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) crew will be a defining characteristic of future deep-space exploration missions. This inherent communication lag necessitates a substantial increase in crew autonomy to ensure mission success and crew safety. Addressing this critical need, the Joint Augmented Reality (AR) team at NASA’s Johnson Space Center (JSC) has developed a novel concept for an augmented reality informatics display specifically designed for integration into EVA suits. This Joint AR system aims to empower crew members to make independent decisions using local resources, aligning with NASA’s objectives to enhance both crew autonomy and interaction with ground teams in future human planetary exploration missions.

records.title: First Lunar Farside SETI Observations for Periodic Signals with the Low-frequency Radio Spectrometer of Chang'E-4 Mission
records.summary: Chang'E-4 (CE4), the first mission to soft-land on the lunar farside, provides a unique opportunity for astronomical observations from an environment shielded from terrestrial radio interference, and thus serves as pathfinder for lunar farside radio search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) studies. We present a search for periodic technosignatures using low-frequency radio observations from the CE-4 mission, the first radio SETI study based on data from on the observation in lunar farside. We analyze the CE4 dynamic spectra with a component-level framework that combines principal component analysis (PCA), cross-antenna basis alignment, as well as temporal periodicity and frequency comb structure diagnostics. No final periodic candidate signal is found after the selection procedure, and we therefore find no evidence in the present CE4 sample for a credible periodic artificial signal. This study serves as a pathfinder and provides a practical framework for lunar radio SETI analysis. As more future lunar missions begin to incorporate radio instrumentation, lunar farside may become a promising site for expanding radio SETI research.

records.title: Fly Me to the Moon: Family Conferencing with Communication Delays on Lunar Missions
records.summary: BACKGROUND Current astronauts on the International Space Station have scheduled time to connect with their families via virtual audio and video private family conferences (PFCs). However, one-way communication delays expected to range from 4 to 12 seconds during lunar missions represent a significant paradigm shift for PFCs which have thus far operated with real-time communication. The objective of this study was to determine the effect of lunar communication delays on the expected benefits of PFCs in astronaut-like participants and their families. METHODS Thirty-five primary participants were recruited to approximate astronaut demographics at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. They were asked to identify a family member living outside of Houston to join as their study partner. Each study pair participated in six weekly virtual audiovisual PFC sessions conducted under 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, or 12 second one-way delays. Relationship and individual well-being outcomes were assessed before and after each PFC. Communication quality was assessed after each PFC in reference to the delay implemented. Linear mixed models with planned contrasts examined the impact of each PFC on relationship, individual well-being, and communication quality. RESULTS PFCs improved relationship outcomes relative to baseline regardless of the delay. Compared to PFCs with no delays, greater decrements to relationships and individual well-being were observed after PFCs with 8 second one-way delays or longer. Participants also indicated all delay latencies significantly reduced their communication quality and would impact their relationships if they were required to continue communicating under those conditions for six months. CONCLUSION PFCs benefit long distance relationships among astronaut-like families. While participants generally tolerated shorter communication delays in this time limited laboratory setting, our results suggest that PFCs with communication delays, especially 8 seconds or longer, may not be sufficient to maintain family bonds in future long duration lunar missions. These findings underscore the importance of maintaining access to family and friends during spaceflight and provide a foundation from which innovative solutions can be crafted to preserve connections despite obstacles to communication.
keywords: Space Communications, Spacecraft Communications, Command and Tracking

records.title: FPGA-Accelerated Precision Time Protocol
records.summary: This IRAD proposes to demonstrate an FPGA-accelerated implementation of Precision Time Protocol (PTP) v2.1 achieving sub microsecond accuracy for distributed spacecraft and lunar surface systems, addressing a critical gap in Earth-independent exploration infrastructure. Current approaches, Pulse-Per-Second (PPS) and Network Time Protocol (NTP), lack either absolute time distribution or necessary precision for autonomous coordination of distributed assets. PTP v2.1 delivers over 1000 times greater accuracy than NTP through hardware-timestamping at the physical layer, providing a robust timescale format with UTC offset support that enables Lunar Time Coordinated (LTC) distribution across lunar infrastructure. By developing flight-optimized FPGA components implementing frequency and phase correction in hardware, this effort establishes a reusable architecture deployable from individual spacecraft to distributed lunar networks, directly supporting ASSET Priority #5: "Exploration Enabling Systems" and enabling the sub microsecond time synchronization required for coordinated robotic operations, distributed sensor fusion, precision localization, and coordinated power distribution without Earth-in-the-loop commanding. Building on Goddard's heritage in flight-proven FPGA implementations and role in LCRNS architecture development, this IRAD matures precision timing capabilities essential for NASA's Ignition Initiative lunar surface operations, positioning Goddard as the center of excellence for timing infrastructure in Earth-independent exploration. Benefits: FPGA-accelerated PTP v2.1 achieving sub microsecond accuracy for distributed spacecraft and lunar surface systems; reusable architecture from individual spacecraft to distributed lunar networks; enables Lunar Time Coordinated (LTC) distribution across lunar infrastructure; >1000× greater accuracy than NTP.
keywords: Communications, Navigation, and Orbital Debris Tracking and Characterization Systems

records.title: Full Stack Navigation, Mapping, and Planning for the Lunar Autonomy Challenge
records.summary: We present a modular, full-stack autonomy system for lunar surface navigation and mapping developed for the Lunar Autonomy Challenge. Operating in a GNSS-denied, visually challenging environment, our pipeline integrates semantic segmentation, stereo visual odometry, pose graph SLAM with loop closures, and layered planning and control. We leverage lightweight learning-based perception models for real-time segmentation and feature tracking and use a factor-graph backend to maintain globally consistent localization. High-level waypoint planning is designed to promote mapping coverage while encouraging frequent loop closures, and local motion planning uses arc sampling with geometric obstacle checks for efficient, reactive control. We evaluate our approach in the competition's high-fidelity lunar simulator, demonstrating centimeter-level localization accuracy, high-fidelity map generation, and strong repeatability across random seeds and rock distributions. Our solution achieved first place in the final competition evaluation.

records.title: GNSS-based Lunar Orbit and Clock Estimation With Stochastic Cloning UD Filter
records.summary: This paper presents a terrestrial GNSS-based orbit and clock estimation framework for lunar navigation satellites. To enable high-precision estimation under the low-observability conditions encountered at lunar distances, we develop a stochastic-cloning UD-factorized filter and delayed-state smoother that provide enhanced numerical stability when processing precise time-differenced carrier phase (TDCP) measurements. A comprehensive dynamics and measurement model is formulated, explicitly accounting for relativistic coupling between orbital and clock states, lunar time-scale transformations, and signal propagation delays including ionospheric, plasmaspheric, and Shapiro effects. The proposed approach is evaluated using high-fidelity Monte-Carlo simulations incorporating realistic multi-constellation GNSS geometry, broadcast ephemeris errors, lunar satellite dynamics, and ionospheric and plasmaspheric delay computed from empirical electron density models. Simulation results demonstrate that combining ionosphere-free pseudorange and TDCP measurements achieves meter-level orbit accuracy and sub-millimeter-per-second velocity accuracy, satisfying the stringent signal-in-space error requirements of future Lunar Augmented Navigation Services (LANS).

records.title: High-Altitude Balloon (HAB) Flight Testing of a Flat-Panel K/Ka-Band Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) for Multi-User Relay in Lunar Communication Architectures.
records.summary: Bent-pipe relay architecture treats a satellite or aerial platform as a non-regenerative radio-frequency repeater, where uplink signals are amplified, frequency translated, and retransmitted without onboard processing. This approach significantly reduces complexity, power consumption, and cost of the payload irrespective of the modulation and waveform formats. As a result, bent-pipe relays are well suited for small satellite platforms, such as CubeSats, where size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints are critical. High-altitude balloon (HAB) aerial platforms, e.g., stratospheric balloons, provide a practical means of validating such relay architectures by offering wide-area line-of-sight coverage and a cost-effective analog to orbital systems. These platforms enable realistic testing of relay performance, beamforming, and multi-user communication links without the need for space deployment and are increasingly considered as part of space–air–ground integrated network (SAGIN) architectures.

records.title: High-Fidelity Baseline Design and Station Keeping Analyses for Earth-Moon Vertical Orbits
records.summary: Earth-Moon vertical orbits are periodic solutions of the circular restricted three-body problem (CR3BP) with substantial out-of-plane motion, considered for high-latitude lunar observation and cislunar navigation. This work develops an end-to-end framework for high-fidelity reference generation under rotating-frame geometry constraints and receding-horizon model predictive control. A representative $L_2$ vertical orbit yields a 5.5-year reference with negligible deterministic correction and remains maintainable in five-year Monte Carlo simulations under realistic uncertainties. The workflow produces locally optimal solutions across 90 consecutive daily start epochs and 200 catalog cases. Finite-Time Lyapunov Exponent along the reference and stable/unstable CR3BP directions interpret station-keeping behavior.

records.title: High-Sensitivity, Large-Doppler-Range DSSS-GMSK Signal Acquisition Algorithm for Earth-Moon Space Satellite Communication
records.summary: With the intensifying competition among countries in lunar and deep-space exploration, the forward communication bands between Earth and the Moon are becoming increasingly congested. Spread-spectrum communication is poised to replace conventional unified-carrier wave systems as the dominant telemetry and tracking technology. Compared with Phase-Shift Keying (PSK) modulation, Gaussian-Filtered Minimum-Shift Keying (GMSK) offers lower transmit sidelobes and higher spectral efficiency, making it a promising alternative to Quadrature Phase-Shift Keying (QPSK) as a communication scheme integrated with spread-spectrum systems. This paper compares the direct-sequence spread-spectrum Gaussian-Filtered Minimum-Shift Keying (DSSS-GMSK) modulation scheme with the widely adopted DSSS-BPSK scheme and demonstrates the advantages of DSSS-GMSK, including higher spectral efficiency and improved signal acquisition performance over a wide Doppler dynamic range. This paper also proposes a deep-space DSSS-GMSK signal acquisition algorithm capable of achieving signal acquisition at a carrier-to-noise density ratio (C/N0) of 34 dB-Hz over a Doppler range from -350 kHz to +350 kHz, demonstrating the feasibility and potential of DSSS-GMSK. The algorithm requires minimal computational hardware resources, and its feasibility has been verified through simulations. Furthermore, its resistance to false locking is analyzed and discussed.

records.title: Human-Centered Design of Next-Generation Telemetry Displays for NASA’s Moon and Mars Exploration Missions
records.summary: NASA’s upcoming Artemis lunar surface missions will significantly increase telemetry volume and operational demands for Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) operations team in NASA’s Mission Control Center (MCC). These missions require telemetry displays that more effectively support real-time monitoring, situational awareness, and decision making than existing International Space Station (ISS) systems, which were not designed for sustained lunar surface operations or the expanded telemetry demands of modern exploration architectures. The objective of this paper is to identify human-centered design requirements for next-generation Artemis EVA telemetry displays that can be implemented within existing mission control constraints. The study integrates human factors principles from high-risk operational domains with qualitative feedback (N=10) from flight controllers, flight instructors and backroom regarding current display strengths, limitations and desired capabilities. Responses were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring usability challenges and operational needs. The results reveal key limitations of current telemetry displays, including dense text-based layouts, limited data correlation, non-intuitive navigation, and high training burden. In response, this paper defines a set of actionable design requirements emphasizing layered information hierarchies, synoptic schematic displays, contextual filtering, multimodal alerting, intuitive navigation, and selective automation. These findings provide practical, near-term guidance for developing Artemis EVA telemetry displays that function as cognitive support tools rather than passive data repositories, reducing controller workload and enhancing situational awareness to support safe and effective lunar surface operations.

records.title: Inspiralling Binary merger parameter reconstruction with lunar and satellite Laser Ranging
records.summary: Precision tracking of Earth--Moon and Earth--satellite ranges offers a novel, low-frequency avenue for detecting gravitational waves from inspiralling massive black hole binaries, complementary to space-based interferometers. In this paper, we propose a first study of the reconstruction of the binary parameters from a synthetic set of range observations. \textit{Set-up}: Assuming an ideal unperturbed Keplerian motion for the earth-satellite binary, we develop a framework for reconstructing the chirp mass $\mathcal M_c$ and luminosity distance $D_L$ of chirping sources from the perturbations they induce on ranging observables, using both Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) and a two-satellite ranging configuration (GUEST) as concrete case studies. \textit{Result}: We find that chirp-mass recovery tightly converges as a power law in SNR ($σ_{M_c}/M_c \propto \mathrm{SNR}^α$, $α\simeq -1$ to $-1.8$) for both LLR and GUEST. In contrast, the luminosity distance suffers from a severe, SNR-independent degeneracy with the sky-orientation angles in the LLR configuration, yielding fractional biases and uncertainties of tens to over a hundred percent regardless of signal strength. The two-satellite GUEST configuration breaks this degeneracy and restores a convergent, SNR-dependent recovery of $D_L$ comparable in scaling to that of the chirp mass. These results demonstrate that multi-baseline ranging architectures are essential for extracting luminosity-distance information from ranging-based gravitational wave searches, while chirp-mass measurements remain reliably accessible even with a single ranging baseline such as the Earth--Moon system.

records.title: Korean lunar navigation constellation with stability-filtered optimisation
records.summary: The international lunar navigation baseline-eight satellites in elliptical lunar frozen orbits (ELFOs) with [Formula: see text]-provides robust south-polar PNT coverage but leaves near-side mid-latitudes largely unserved. This gap directly affects the Korea Aerospace Administration (KASA) 2032 lander mission, whose candidate sites span latitudes [Formula: see text]-[Formula: see text]. We propose the Korean Lunar Navigation System (KLNS): five augmentation satellites in [Formula: see text] ELFOs that concentrate dwell time over the northern hemisphere. A two-stage optimisation is employed. First, every candidate orbit in a 10,368-element search space is propagated for 720 hours under a perturbed model (lunar [Formula: see text] + Earth third-body) and screened against four stability criteria, removing 2864 (27.6%) dynamically infeasible candidates. Second, a greedy sequential algorithm with hard S-ROI protection selects five KLNS satellites that raise N40-70 PNT availability from 0.0 to 89.5%, far exceeding the 50% target, while preserving 99.7% south-polar coverage. The stability-filtered greedy solution outperforms a [Formula: see text] genetic-algorithm benchmark (85.6%), demonstrating that a well-designed pre-filter can obviate more expensive metaheuristics. Site-specific evaluation confirms 92.5-94.2% availability at all three northern KASA candidate landing sites under the augmented constellation.

records.title: LuMon: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Development Suite with Novel Datasets for Lunar Monocular Depth Estimation
records.summary: Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is crucial for autonomous lunar rover navigation using electro-optical cameras. However, deploying terrestrial MDE networks to the Moon brings a severe domain gap due to harsh shadows, textureless regolith, and zero atmospheric scattering. Existing evaluations rely on analogs that fail to replicate these conditions and lack actual metric ground truth. To address this, we present LuMon, a comprehensive benchmarking framework to evaluate MDE methods for lunar exploration. We introduce novel datasets featuring high-quality stereo ground truth depth from the real Chang'e-3 mission and the CHERI dark analog dataset. Utilizing this framework, we conduct a systematic zero-shot evaluation of state-of-the-art architectures across synthetic, analog, and real datasets. We rigorously assess performance against mission critical challenges like craters, rocks, extreme shading, and varying depth ranges. Furthermore, we establish a sim-to-real domain adaptation baseline by fine tuning a foundation model on synthetic data. While this adaptation yields drastic in-domain performance gains, it exhibits minimal generalization to authentic lunar imagery, highlighting a persistent cross-domain transfer gap. Our extensive analysis reveals the inherent limitations of current networks and sets a standard foundation to guide future advancements in extraterrestrial perception and domain adaptation.

records.title: Lunar Reflective Interferometry
records.summary: We present the method of lunar reflection interferometry (LRI) in which a virtual interferometer can be formed by using a spacecraft-borne antenna in lunar orbit that receives both direct rays and those reflected from the lunar surface. The technique exploits the method of images and is akin to the classic "sea cliff" interferometer, with the Moon's surface, primarily the lunar Maria, replacing the ocean surface. We describe the method in detail, demonstrate that significant portions of the Moon's surface are sufficiently smooth at low radio frequencies, $ν\lesssim 10\,\mathrm{MHz}$, for the technique to work, and outline a spacecraft instrument implementation. We describe potential systematic errors and how they could be mitigated. We present several astrophysics applications of the method.

records.title: Lunar RNSS Out-of-Band Interference AFS Use Case
records.summary: Lunar Communication Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) will enable communication and navigation services through a combination of servicing satellites orbiting the moon. On the lunar surface, these services will coexist with Wi-Fi and cellular wireless (3GPP). The LunaNet Interoperability Specification (LNIS) outlines the design for the GNSS-like Augmented Forward Signal (AFS) and Lunar Augmented Navigation Service (LANS), enabling orbiting and surface users in lunar space, such as Artemis missions, to estimate their position, velocity, and time (LNIS, 2025). As described by J-L Isler et al. (ION GNSS+, 2025), the 2483.5-2500 MHz band has been established for Lunar PNT. Adjacent wireless (Wi-Fi and 3GPP) bands for communication on the moon are assigned to be 3.5 MHz away on either side of the band, resulting in high-power emissions in near proximity to the AFS navigation band. This is particularly the case for AFS receivers on the lunar surface collocated with (or near) wireless devices. By comparison, Ligado (formerly LightSquared) had planned to operate with a guard band 24 MHz away from L1, which was considered to be too close for many commercial GPS receivers due to practical limits on receiver filtering and front-end bandwidth, even for receivers operating 14 km away from a 29 dBW L-band cellular base station. The S-band allocation is foreseen to be used for LunaNet-compatible and other systems alike, meaning that the spectrum interference challenges identified here will affect multiple lunar communication and navigation systems. The current spectrum allocation allows the operation of a wireless system at ≥ 2503.5 MHz for 3GPP cellular communications and ≤ 2480 MHz for Wi-Fi. To adequately investigate the feasibility of operating just 3.5 MHz away, this work conducts an end-to-end feasibility study of the impact of high-power adjacent band wireless interference. First, tests were conducted on commercial L5 and L1 band GPS receivers to investigate their response to high-power interference adjacent to the GPS band and determine rejection typical of commercial receivers at L-band to infer requirements for S-band. These tests were conducted as a function of guard-band distance to emulate the effect of interference that is only 3.5 MHz away from a band edge. The results demonstrated that 3.5 MHz is not adequate to reject interference for both wide band receivers tracking L5 in its 24 MHz band and narrow band receivers tracking C/A code in the 30.69 MHz GPS L1 band, which is nearly twice the size of the band used by AFS. Secondly, a model of a high-performance receiver front end was constructed based on Hegarty (ION Navigation, 2020). The model was reworked using various combinations of available S-band components, including LNAs, SAW filters, Intermediate frequency (IF) filters, and a cavity filter. A custom filter was also specified as a variant of one of SAWTRON’s commercial products. The effect of aliasing due to out-of-band interference ...

records.title: Lunar Silicon Cavity
records.summary: The Moon's permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) are among the coldest places in the Solar System and are expected to become key landing sites for upcoming international space agency missions. Their proximity to peaks of perpetual solar power and potential resource richness makes them prime candidates for lunar exploration and future Moon bases. Here we propose to deploy a passive, ultrastable optical resonator in these regions that will enable laser systems with unprecedented phase-coherence. The unique physical environment of lunar PSRs greatly benefits the construction of a cryogenic monolithic silicon cavity that exhibits low $10^{-18}$ thermal noise-limited stability and coherence time exceeding 1 minute, more than a decade better than the current best terrestrial system. Such a stable laser will form an enabling infrastructure for quantum technology in space to serve many applications, including establishing a lunar time standard, building long-baseline optical interferometry, distribution of stable optical signals across networks of satellites, testing general relativity and gravitational physics, and forming the backbone for space-based quantum networks.
